To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

an abnormal respiratory rate (either low or high) is a highly reliable predictor (sensitivity 95%, specificity 97% and positive predictive value 97%) of life-threatening clinical deterioration, and that a respiratory rate of 30 per minute is the best threshold to use for triggering a medical emergency team (MET).
an abnormal respiratory rate (either high or low) is a highly reliable predictor for the occurrence of a life-threatening clinical event in the next 24 hours in a general medical ward.

an abnormal respiratory rate (either high or low) is a highly reliable predictor for life-threatening events, and that the reliability of the other vital signs for predicting life-threatening events is poor.

the vital signs of patients in hospital.
the use of vital signs as a trigger to activate a medical emergency team.
the vital signs, and the medical emergency team.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vital signs are vital, and that vital signs are important.
vital signs, especially heart rate, are a highly reliable indicator of life-threatening clinical instability.
vital signs are a vital part of the patient assessment process, and should be monitored in all hospitalised patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the use of vital signs as a trigger to identify patients in whom there are life-threatening clinical events is a reliable and cost-effective method of identifying those patients.
we have demonstrated that vital signs are a simple but highly sensitive and specific marker of the need for urgent intervention in the acutely ill medical patient.

vital signs are an extremely useful tool in the early detection of patients at risk of clinical deterioration, and that a system of continuous vital signs monitoring is a highly reliable predictor for life-threatening clinical events in hospital patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the vital signs are an important part of the patient’s story, and they should be recorded and interpreted by all clinicians, including emergency physicians, who are involved in the management of the critically ill patient.
the vital signs are a very sensitive predictor of life-threatening events.
the simple vital signs of heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and temperature are a highly reliable early warning system for life-threatening events.
